title: Randomized APSP hypothesis for polynomial integer weights
formal: Is the following hypothesis true? \[\forall\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \exists c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \neg\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] Here \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) means that a uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the entire exact distance matrix of every directed \(n\)-vertex graph with integer edge weights in \([-n^c,n^c]\) and no negative-weight cycle, succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input, and has worst-case time \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) over all inputs and coin sequences. The word model and the quantifiers hidden in this definition are specified below. The weight exponent \(c\) may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This makes explicit the weaker quantifier order stated in the 2026 source; the 2018 source's phrase about sufficiently large \(c\) did not specify that dependence.
why: The randomized APSP hypothesis is a principal foundation of fine-grained complexity. Resolving it would determine whether exact distances in general integer-weighted graphs admit a fixed polynomial improvement over cubic time, and would affect a large network of conditional bounds for graph, matrix, sequence and dynamic problems.
status_note: The original 2018 source states the randomized polynomial-integer-weight hypothesis. Fischer's 29 March 2026 full preprint explicitly states the modern forall-epsilon/exists-c formulation adopted here as Hypothesis 1.1, describes truly subcubic APSP as a major open question, and fixes the randomized word-RAM model. A bounded primary-source review through 16 September 2026, including the 2025 few-weight results, the conditional 2026 universe reduction, July 2026 node-weighted-triangle work and the August 2026 reduction barrier, found no verified resolution of this exact statement. This does not exhaustively certify current openness. The stronger quantifier order with one absolute c for every epsilon is not silently substituted for this target.

importance.reason: A core fine-grained hardness hypothesis for a basic graph problem, including randomized algorithms and polynomial integer weights. Its extensive graph and matrix equivalences and consequences for other algorithmic problems make a resolution foundational. This individual assessment is based on that breadth and the precise target, not the inherited provisional score or the existence of a survey entry.

sentences: All-pairs shortest paths asks for the exact distance between every ordered pair of vertices in a directed graph.
The graph has polynomially bounded signed integer edge weights and no negative-weight cycle.
The hypothesis says that for every fixed improvement over the cubic exponent, some polynomial weight bound rules out every randomized algorithm with that running time.
Computation uses logarithmic-size machine words, and the whole distance matrix must be correct with probability at least two thirds on every input.
Known general algorithms save a subpolynomial factor, while recent restricted algorithms and conditional equivalences do not settle this hypothesis.

definitions:
For fixed integers \(n\ge2\) and \(c\ge1\), the vertex set is \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). The input is \(n\) and an \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix in vertex order, with a presence flag for each ordered pair and, for each present edge, a signed integer weight \(w(u,v)\) satisfying \(|w(u,v)|\le n^c\). There is at most one edge per ordered pair; self-loops are allowed. Missing edges are indicated by their flags. The graph is promised to have no directed cycle with negative total weight. Negative edges, zero-weight cycles and ties between shortest paths are allowed. For vertices \(u,v\), let \(d_G(u,v)\) be the minimum total weight of a finite directed walk from \(u\) to \(v\), or a separate unreachable symbol \(+\infty\) if there is no such walk. The empty walk has weight zero. Under the promise every reachable minimum is attained, \(d_G(u,u)=0\), and each finite distance has absolute value at most \((n-1)n^c\). The output consists of these \(n^2\) exact integers or unreachable flags in vertex-pair order; listing all path vertices is not required.

The machine is a word RAM with one fixed finite program. For a fixed integer \(a\ge c+4\), its word length on \(n\)-vertex inputs is \(b(n)=\lceil a\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) bits. Each memory address and memory cell is one word. The input is one word for n followed in row-major order by two words for each matrix entry: its zero-or-one presence flag and its signed weight, with zero in the weight word when the flag is zero. The output uses the same row-major order and two words per entry: a zero-or-one finite-distance flag and its signed distance, with zero in the second word for unreachable pairs. Signed integers use two's-complement encoding; distances fit in a constant number of words. Word load, store, copy, comparison, conditional branch, bitwise Boolean operations, shifts, and addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b(n)}\) each cost one step. Unsigned quotient and remainder by a nonzero word also cost one step. Division by zero is invalid; shifts by at least \(b(n)\) positions return zero. Algorithms may use several words for larger quantities, charging all operations. All accessed addresses must fit in a word. Work memory initially contains zero, and no input-dependent precomputed tables, advice or oracle are supplied. All preprocessing, table construction, memory operations and output writing count toward the time bound. One random instruction yields one fresh independent fair bit in one step. The input graph is fixed before the coins are drawn. Deterministic programs are included by ignoring random bits.

Precisely, \(\mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon)\) asserts the existence of a finite program \(A\), an integer word-size factor \(a\ge c+4\), and an integer constant \(C\ge1\), such that for every integer \(n\ge2\) and every promised graph, every run halts within \(Cn^{3-\varepsilon}\) steps, and with probability at least \(2/3\) its entire output matrix equals \((d_G(u,v))_{u,v\in[n]}\). Correctness is joint for the matrix, rather than a separate bound for each entry. The program, \(a\) and \(C\) may depend on the fixed \(c\) and \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(n\) or the input graph. There is no requirement to classify or detect inputs that violate the promise. The exponent in the time bound concerns the number \(n\) of vertices; the input has \(\Theta(n^2)\) words and \(O(n^2\log n)\) bits for each fixed \(c,a\). Rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\) capture every possible fixed positive exponent saving.
answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed hypothesis, or of its full logical negation \[\exists\varepsilon\in\mathbb Q\cap(0,1]\ \forall c\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}:\ \mathrm{FastAPSP}(c,\varepsilon).\] A refutation must therefore establish one common positive exponent saving for every fixed polynomial weight bound; programs and runtime constants may depend on \(c\). A proof of the hypothesis must rule out all uniform randomized algorithms in the specified model for a suitable \(c\) at each saving \(\varepsilon\). A deterministic-only lower bound, a barrier for a particular algorithm or reduction technique, or a truly subcubic algorithm only for one restricted weight regime does not settle the statement. Neither do approximate distances, random input distributions, single-source bounds, distributed round bounds or extra accurate predictions. A subpolynomial-factor improvement over cubic time alone is insufficient. This yes/no target concerns exact APSP algorithms; an unproved APSP hypothesis cannot be assumed as the proof of itself.

context_blocks.text: The 2018 survey treats APSP as one of the central hypotheses used to explain polynomial-time barriers. Its model permits randomization and logarithmic machine words, and its graph weights are polynomially bounded signed integers with no negative cycle.

Fischer's 2026 formulation explicitly places the requested exponent saving before the weight exponent: for every saving there is a polynomial weight range that remains hard. Its footnote distinguishes the stronger hypothesis with one absolute weight exponent for all savings. The paper uses nonnegative weights and explicitly states equivalence with the signed, no-negative-cycle convention retained here.

Williams gives a randomized word-RAM algorithm for nonnegative integer weights bounded by \(M\) in time \(n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}+n^{2+o(1)}\log M\). For polynomial \(M\), this achieves a substantial improvement over cubic time while the saving remains subpolynomial in \(n\), so it does not provide a fixed exponent improvement.

The 2025 few-weights algorithms exploit a bound on the number of distinct edge weights associated with each vertex. Their truly subcubic results concern those restricted instances, whereas this hypothesis imposes no such bound.

The 2026 universe-reduction paper connects APSP to stronger hypotheses for small-weight and unweighted graphs. Its full equivalence is conditional on the matrix-multiplication exponent being two and on an additional algorithmic assumption from additive combinatorics; it proves neither the APSP hypothesis nor its negation.

The August 2026 lower bound concerns a class of black-box triangle reductions. It limits those reductions' ability to preserve precise running-time exponents, and does not establish a general lower bound for APSP algorithms.

This inert draft contains no canonical, queue, selection, comment, commit or publication mutation. Preserve the existing category and original notes/comments.

Recovered source exactly: author survey eccentri.pdf, PDF p. 5 defines polynomially bounded integer edge weights and excludes negative cycles; Hypothesis 3 on PDF p. 6 excludes randomized O(n^{3-epsilon}) algorithms for sufficiently large c; pp. 3–4 specify logarithmic-word RAM. The source does not explicitly quantify c relative to epsilon or enumerate its RAM instruction set and success probability. The draft makes those conventions visible rather than claiming they were literally written there.

The key later source is Fischer 2026, arXiv:2603.27736v1, Hypothesis 1.1 and footnote 3 on printed p. 1/PDF p. 3. It explicitly adopts forall epsilon > 0 exists c, and distinguishes the stronger exists c forall epsilon > 0 formulation. Parent approved using the weaker explicitly sourced formulation and publicly disclosing the ambiguity of the 2018 wording. No equivalence between these two quantifier orders is asserted. Taking c to be a positive integer is harmless by rounding a finite real exponent upward and monotonicity of the input family. Similarly, sufficiently large c can be expressed by existence because hardness persists upon enlarging the admissible weight range.

Negation audit: the target is forall epsilon exists c not Fast(c,epsilon), so its full negation is exists epsilon forall c Fast(c,epsilon). Each c may have its own finite algorithm, word-size constant and runtime constant, while the same positive saving epsilon must work for every c. Merely giving different positive savings epsilon_c tending to zero with c does not refute this formulation. The card does not strengthen the negation by requiring a compiler that takes c as input and produces algorithms.

The directed model is explicit in Fischer footnote 1; original APSP permits directed graphs. The signed weights and no-negative-cycle promise are preserved from 2018 rather than silently changed to nonnegative or unit weights. Fischer footnote 2 states the equivalence of its nonnegative convention to signed weights via a potential reweighting and a sufficiently fast single-source computation. Such normalization may enlarge the polynomial weight exponent, which is allowed by the chosen quantifiers. No equivalence to the fixed-small-weight Strong APSP hypothesis is assumed.

Definitions include a dense explicit matrix, at most one directed edge per ordered pair, possible self-loops, missing-edge flags, zero-weight ties/cycles, unreachable pairs, empty paths, all n^2 exact outputs, and the lack of any requirement to detect a violated negative-cycle promise. Distances of reachable distinct vertices have a simple-path witness with at most n-1 edges, so they fit in O(log n) bits for fixed c. They are not real-valued inputs or approximate outputs. The 1/100 numerical benchmark rule does not change the computational problem inside this yes/no hypothesis.

The finite-program word-RAM convention is a concrete editorial completion of the source's standard logarithmic-word RAM. Word-size factors may depend on fixed c and the algorithm, keeping every word O(log n) bits and permitting all weights and addresses in O(1) words. The explicit instruction set has only conventional word operations; multiword arithmetic, preprocessing, generated tables, random bits and output are charged. It supplies no unbounded-precision real primitive, arbitrary-real advice, nonuniform lookup table or cryptographic/quantum oracle. Using fair words rather than fair bits or simulating word multiplication/division with simpler bit operations changes costs by at most polylogarithmic factors; with a possible smaller epsilon, this preserves whether a fixed truly subcubic saving exists.

Probability/time normalization: Fischer Section 2.5 (printed p. 15/PDF p. 17) allows randomized algorithms succeeding with probability 1-n^{-d} for arbitrarily large constant d. The draft chooses joint matrix success 2/3 and a worst-case bound for every coin sequence. Repeating independently and taking a coordinatewise majority increases whole-matrix success: whenever a majority of complete runs are correct, every coordinate majority is correct. O(log n) repetitions give high probability, adding O(n^2 log n) output-comparison cost and preserving truly subcubic existence after shrinking epsilon. Conversely high probability implies constant success, after harmless treatment of finitely many sizes. These equivalences concern the existence of some positive saving, not equality of one fixed epsilon predicate.

Expected-time variants also do not change the full no-truly-subcubic hypothesis under conventional bounded error: first amplify success to at least 5/6 by a constant number of repetitions, then abort after a sufficiently large constant multiple of the worst-case-over-input expected runtime. Markov's inequality bounds abort probability by at most 1/6, giving joint success at least 2/3 and a worst-case runtime bound. Conversely a worst-case bound implies the same expected bound. The draft itself fixes worst-case time explicitly; it does not confuse average input distributions with per-input randomization. This normalization is an audit explanation, not a proposed APSP solution technique.

Verified Williams' exact Theorem 1.1 in arXiv:1312.6680v2, PDF p. 3: Monte Carlo word-RAM time n^3/2^{Omega(sqrt(log n))}+n^{2+o(1)} log M for nonnegative weights. For M=n^c with fixed c, the second term is lower order and the saving is n^{o(1)}, not a fixed n^epsilon. The theorem's expanded 2018 journal proof was not separately audited. The 2026 universe paper still identifies this as the best known general bound at its date.

Bounded later review checked the actual 2025 few-weight paper's input definition and main results, rather than inferring a full solution from the title. Checked Fischer's actual 2026 Theorem 1.13 and critical remarks: its full APSP/Strong APSP/unweighted equivalence assumes both omega=2 and a sum-order-preserving hashing hypothesis with polynomial bounds. It does not settle APSP. Also read the July 2026 ICALP node-weighted-triangle introduction/Theorem 1/Corollary 2, DOI 10.4230/LIPIcs.ICALP.2026.10: vertex weights are a restriction and the result is not arbitrary edge-weighted APSP. Finally, the actual August 2026 black-box reduction paper's Definition 1 and Theorem 1 restrict a class of reductions for arbitrary relations; it cannot be called an unconditional APSP lower bound. Cached sources have prefix apsp-hyp-.

Duplication audit read the current TCS-6510 formal statement, definitions, answer criterion and sources. Despite the request's deterministic-versus-randomized concern, that card currently itself permits randomization; its real distinction is arbitrary real weights in a comparison-addition real RAM. It is not just this integer word-RAM hypothesis with opposite polarity. Here integer digits and word operations on weights are accessible; there the representation of real values cannot be inspected. Conversely an unrestricted real-addition computation can create intermediate values whose bit lengths preclude an automatic constant-time word simulation. No exact equivalence of these fully specified models was verified, so automatic merging or an unqualified implication is unsupported. TCS-7347 asks a different threshold for directed unweighted APSP, while TCS-0478 is dynamic. Existing related IDs TCS-3123 and TCS-6940 had no corresponding current data/cards JSON file when checked; the draft leaves related IDs to the parent's repository-level validation rather than mutating them.

Importance was previously unassessed at 50. Recommend 97 independently: this is a central randomized fine-grained assumption for general integer-weighted graphs, with widespread consequences and source-documented equivalences. Its conceptual scope is not a minor parameter refinement. Preserve category. Source-open status is qualified to the exact modern quantifier formulation and bounded literature review, not an exhaustive proof that no solution exists.
